final.title: Afforestation as a mitigation strategy: countering climate-induced risk of forest carbon sink in China
final.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background
                    
                      China has made substantial efforts in afforestation since the 1970s, significantly contributing to the country’s forest carbon sink. However, the future carbon sink dynamics remain uncertain due to anticipated changes in forest age structure, climate conditions, and atmospheric CO
                      2
                      concentrations. Moreover, the extent to which afforestation can enhance future carbon sequestration has not been fully quantified. This study focuses specifically on China and integrates forest growth models with Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) models to project future carbon dynamics based on shifts in forest habitat suitability. A nature scenario is applied to evaluate potential climate-induced risks to forest carbon sequestration, while an afforestation scenario is used to assess the additional contribution from planned afforestation efforts.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results

final.title: The role of the Voluntary Carbon Market in addressing global social challenges: ecological (in)justice in Africa’s largest REDD+ project?
final.abstract:
The sheer existence of the Loss and Damage Fund is an acknowledgement of the asymmetry between the causes and effects of climate change, with those countries least responsible the hardest hit. The funds pledged at COP28 amount to less than 2 per cent of the amount needed. Most alarmingly, more than half of climate finance reported by wealthy countries for the period 2011–20 was
                    redirected development aid
                    , undermining delivery on other pressing priorities. The need to augment public sources of finance with private is apparent, yet triggers debates around the ‘commodification of nature’ and the suitability of market mechanisms to deliver social and environmental outcomes. Through case study research in Zambia’s Luangwa Valley, home to the largest REDD+ project in Africa, I interrogate the extent to which capital pursues financial efficiencies over development effectiveness. Although there is evidence that the Voluntary Carbon Market can deliver a price that includes benefits ‘beyond carbon’, the opacity in over-the-counter sales fuels suspicion that communities may not be receiving their fair share. In addition, the fragmented policy environment emerges as a key driver of deforestation while weak local governance erodes trust, with allegations of elite capture commonplace. Nonetheless, communities’ desire to retain their forests – and to benefit financially from so doing – is strong, and their voices should not be drowned out in the furore. candidates.title: Applying the greenhouse gas inventory calculation approach to predict the forest carbon sink
candidates.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background
                    Finland’s national Climate Act contains a target for carbon neutrality by 2035. Achieving this target not only depends on the effective implementation of emission reductions, but to a large part on the forest carbon sink. A recent publication of the Government’s analysis, assessment, and research activities highlights a potential disparity in forest land greenhouse gas (GHG) balance estimates by the ex-ante scenario model used in the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP), and the ex-post GHG inventory methodology used for creating an official record of emissions and removals. Better methodological compatibility is needed to answer a key question: How large will the forest carbon sink be in different scenarios? This study is a first attempt to show the usefulness of applying the GHG inventory calculation approach to predict the forest carbon sink.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      In this study, we introduce a tool that can be used to estimate the GHG balance for forest land, what we call a “synthetic inventory”, and validate it by comparing outputs against historical data reported in Finland’s GHG inventory. Second, we use it to predict GHG balances in year leading up to 2035 at various roundwood and forest residue harvest rates. The tool can replicate forest GHG balances for forest land with an average annual error of 1.0 Mt CO
                      2
                      , representing 4% of the average annual forest
